title: Два выходных для Лёвы и визит к Нагиеву  (Two Days Off for Lyova and Visiting Nagiyev)

segments.t: Handing Lyova tickets to Saint Petersburg, Chef Barinov declares that his sous-chef is officially on a two-day holiday and orders him to take his mother on the trip immediately. Meanwhile, Max spots Nagiyev heading into his office and decides to ask the owner for a loan.
А сейчас начался у тебя выходной.
Alright, let's go through it step by step in English.
'But I am on shift at work.' Bringing up the work right here, Barinov reaches for the Russian word "rabote" ("work", built from "rabota") right at the center of the line.
'You were, Lyova.' Speaking candidly with Lyova, spoken Russian compresses the whole thought into just 2 words, skipping the extra helper words English needs.
А сейчас начался у тебя выходной.
'Right now your day off has officially started.' Lyova responds pointedly during the talk, without trying to dress up how he really feels.
'Or rather, two days off.' Highlighting the weekend before Lyova, Barinov centers the thought on "vykhodnykh" ("weekend", from "vykhodnoy") without wasting a word.
'Wait, what about the carrots?' Addressing the carrot around Lyova, Max puts the question word "kak" right at the start so Lyova hears the focus immediately.
'Come on, hurry up and get going.' Lyova answers openly with a sigh, before Max can change the subject.
'What else now?' Barinov follows up directly in front of Max and centers the remark on "yeshchyo" ("more, still") without any extra fuss.
'You wound me, Lyova.' Holding firm promptly in the exchange, spoken Russian compresses the whole thought into just 2 words, skipping the extra helper words English needs.
'We are just hanging out here.' Lyova fires back right away in their talk, watching Max's face to see how the news lands.
'Ah, you are heading in there.' Speaking openly beside Lyova, Barinov links the Russian words directly in the present with no word for "am", "is", or "are" needed.

'There is the man I should borrow money from.' Speaking openly on the spot, Max leans on "nado" ("it is necessary, one needs to"), which carries the whole predicate in Russian without needing "it is".
'So you got all that, Dmitry Vladimirovich?' Lyova probes sharply how Barinov expects that to work in practice.
'What do you want?' Barinov cuts in directly during the talk and puts the emphasis on "nado" ("it is necessary") in the middle of the talk.
А сейчас начался у тебя выходной.
That wraps up this scene as chef Barinov gives Lyova two days off and sends him to Saint Petersburg with his mother, while Max decides to ask Nagiyev for an advance. Until next time!
